title: The Future of Law Firm Business Models in the Age of AI — Jordan Furlong on the Lawyerist Podcast (ep. 607)
pub: Lawyerist Podcast ep. 607, Legal Talk Network (host Stephanie Everett, with Zack Glaser)
author: Jordan Furlong

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: Furlong accepts the need to integrate foundational legal reasoning with practical, human-centred competence and materially develops the cluster’s account by making trustworthy judgment under uncertainty the organising purpose of lawyer training. He also proposes early immersion in listening to and understanding people, while treating his conclusions as provisional rather than empirically established.
qs: The purpose of a lawyer is to deliver reliable, trustworthy judgment and under conditions of uncertainty.
But at the same time, I would be immersing people, aspiring lawyers in that process of meeting people, listening to people, understanding their situation.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core copilot-oriented view that AI changes legal production while preserving human judgment, verification and accountability. It materially develops the proposition by reframing foundational junior-lawyer skills toward checking machine output and by identifying professional character and experience-based judgment as residual sources of legal value, while treating full substitution as possible but less likely.
qs: I’m reasonably confident that we will go down the second road, not the first, but can’t count out the opposite.
They show up differently because to your point, I’m now checking the machines and confirming that work versus doing the first draft and making sure I don’t write and passive voice.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core uncertainty: AI may substitute for substantial legal work while human experience and judgment remain complementary and likely valuable. It materially extends the proposition by identifying bundled insurance as a mechanism that could shift clients from lawyer-in-the-loop advice toward direct reliance on AI, while treating broad displacement as conditional rather than established.
qs: “And if in fact, as I think by the way, will be the case eventually, eventually whether again it’s Clio or Lexis or OpenAI or whomever, when they offer me this package, they also say,” Oh, do you also want to buy an additional $9 a month rider for insurance so that if the advice we give you turns out to not to be good, you can sue us for negligence because that’s common.
I’m reasonably confident that we will go down the second road, not the first, but can’t count out the opposite.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core near-term augmentation model while treating substitution as a contingent risk driven by client trust in insured AI. It materially develops the synthesis by identifying experiential judgment and intensive apprenticeship—observation, debriefing and progressive responsibility—as necessary responses to the redesign of junior work and verification.
qs: I’m reasonably confident that we will go down the second road, not the first, but can’t count out the opposite.

We need experienced lawyers to help new lawyers get over this, especially now to get over this period, to get to the point of, okay, I can figure this out now to develop judgment, to watch what the senior lawyer does, to listen to what’s being said and afterwards to debrief when the senior lawyer says, “Tell me what you saw.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source accepts that AI will shift legal production away from junior lawyers while making human verification and judgment central. It supports intentional retraining in review and evaluative assessment, though it is more optimistic than the cluster that checking AI output can itself develop judgment and does not fully address the loss of independent, hands-on practice.
qs: If you have junior lawyers or have lawyers of any capacity or even contract lawyers, get them into the business of being able to identify, to review, to assess, to evaluate what the AI comes out with and say, “This seems fine.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s framing that AI changes the expertise pipeline rather than straightforwardly eliminating lawyers. It anticipates continued demand for human judgment and explicitly argues that junior training must shift toward verifying machine-generated work while retaining legal writing and analysis skills. Its insured-AI displacement scenario is conditional and reinforces the cluster’s conclusion that long-term substitution remains unsettled.
qs: They show up differently because to your point, I’m now checking the machines and confirming that work versus doing the first draft and making sure I don’t write and passive voice.
I’m going to take this analysis, go to a lawyer, say, here’s what the AI said, but what do you think?

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source supports selective augmentation: AI may supply analysis or drafts, while lawyers retain judgment and verify outputs. It also reinforces the cluster’s junior-development concern by arguing that foundational skills remain necessary but may increasingly be exercised through checking machine-generated work. Its claims are cautious scenarios and professional reasoning, not empirical evidence of productivity or client behaviour.
qs: I’m going to take this analysis, go to a lawyer, say, here’s what the AI said, but what do you think?
They show up differently because to your point, I’m now checking the machines and confirming that work versus doing the first draft and making sure I don’t write and passive voice.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Furlong endorses the cluster’s core view that AI will take over more legal production while lawyers retain supervision, validation and experience-based judgment, and that this shift undermines hourly billing in favour of fixed or recurring fees. He entertains direct AI reliance and broad lawyer displacement as a plausible scenario, but his preferred forecast remains human-in-the-loop legal service rather than autonomous delivery.
qs: And the lawyer’s job will be to supervise that system, to monitor it, to validate its outcomes, and to communicate the impact of those outcomes along with any requested level of judgment or assessment or evaluation that the client might desire.
I’m going to take this analysis, go to a lawyer, say, here’s what the AI said, but what do you think?

kp.k: AI shifts production toward systems and human supervision
kp.d: Furlong argues that legal value production is moving away from extended human task performance toward AI-operated workflows, with lawyers supervising systems, validating outputs and communicating implications and judgment to clients. This is his forecast of changing production and professional roles, rather than a finding supported by empirical research in the transcript.
qs: The workflow will be more or less operated by an artificially intelligence system.

And the lawyer’s job will be to supervise that system, to monitor it, to validate its outcomes, and to communicate the impact of those outcomes along with any requested level of judgment or assessment or evaluation that the client might desire.

kp.k: System access could replace significant staffing costs
kp.d: Furlong predicts that buying or renting workflow systems will replace some reliance on people to carry out legal work. He names Clio, Lexis and Thomson Reuters as possible suppliers and speculates that OpenAI or Anthropic might enter this market. He expects operating costs to become lower and more predictable. Ownership of the resulting profit engine frames the conversation, but private equity and ownership structures are not substantively explored.
qs: I am going to need to be able to buy a system or to rent a system or access to a system, which has all of the capacities that I need in order to, again, operate, monitor, manage the workflow that produces all this kind of work.
Your cost of doing business in a way probably is not only going to go down, but it’s also going to become more certain you will know what you have to spend each year so that you’ve got your baseline.

kp.k: Pricing should follow client value rather than hours
kp.d: Furlong argues that AI performing work in seconds undermines hourly pricing and recommends pricing around client outcomes, the experience of obtaining them and, where relevant, the lawyer-client relationship. He nevertheless expects hourly billing to retain a role in selected novel or high-stakes advocacy matters.
qs: I maintain there will still be uses for the billable hour as a pricing mechanism for select types of work, especially around certain kinds of novel or high stakes advocacy.

The outcome that they received from the relationship they had with you, the experience of gaining that outcome, which includes but is not limited to the price they ended up paying and in certain but not all cases, the relationship with the lawyer, is it one that was positive?

kp.k: Relationships become differentiators as expertise becomes commoditized
kp.d: Furlong predicts that AI will surpass even the strongest human legal expertise within a few years, while allowing possible exceptions for extremely narrow specialisms. He consequently recommends competing through responsiveness, client experience, individuality and care rather than primarily through knowledge. His example of a more responsive lawyer commanding a premium is illustrative, not measured pricing evidence.
qs: We are a very short period of time, a few years away, I would say, from a point where the smartest lawyer in the world is an AI and it’s not even close.

Over the course of your career, I say, who you are and what you’re like to deal with are going to be more important than what you know and what you can do because those last two items are going to be increasingly commoditized, but you cannot find anybody out there who will be the same as you.

kp.k: Trustworthy judgment should anchor professional purpose and licensing
kp.d: Furlong defines professional judgment as helping clients make decisions when they lack clarity or confidence, while leaving the final decision to them. He proposes trustworthy judgment under legal uncertainty as the sole licensing condition and emphasizes integrity and character as foundations of reliability and professional formation. These are normative proposals, not descriptions of existing licensing requirements.
qs: the only condition of licensure for lawyers from now on should be your capacity to have a trustworthy capability to render judgment under uncertainty in legal matters.
It matters that you are a person of character because that’s where a lot of reliability comes from, right?

kp.k: Insured AI advice could displace many human lawyers
kp.d: Furlong presents a conditional scenario in which clients directly rely on AI advice, perhaps supported by insurance. His $20 or $200 monthly access prices and additional $9 monthly insurance rider are hypothetical illustrations, not reported products. He suggests this could threaten much of the profession outside straight advocacy, especially criminal advocacy. Alternatively, clients may bring AI analysis to lawyers for a human assessment; he is reasonably confident in that second path but explicitly does not rule out substitution.
qs: That 20 bucks a month I paid or 200 bucks a month I paid to access this, I’m willing to stake my business or my relationship or something else on that.
Oh, do you also want to buy an additional $9 a month rider for insurance so that if the advice we give you turns out to not to be good, you can sue us for negligence because that’s common.
I think that it would probably take out most everything that’s not straight advocacy and especially criminal advocacy
I’m reasonably confident that we will go down the second road, not the first, but can’t count out the opposite.

kp.k: Legal education needs fundamental redesign around judgment
kp.d: Speaking explicitly from February 2026 and acknowledging his views may change within two years, Furlong criticizes the existing education and licensing model. He asserts that $150,000 and seven years of university education deliver at most one fifth of lawyer competence; the transcript supplies no supporting study. He retains a role for foundational legal knowledge, reasoning, analysis and issue spotting, while recommending early immersion in interviewing, attentive listening and understanding clients.
qs: You cannot charge someone $150,000 to spend seven years getting university education that gets you one fifth maximum the way towards lawyer competence
The purpose of a lawyer going forward, I think right now, February 2026, who knows what I’ll think in two years time.
To the extent that legal education still has any purpose, it is around, number one, laying down a base level of capacity and competence and legal knowledge and reasoning and analysis.
I would be immersing people, aspiring lawyers in that process of meeting people, listening to people, understanding their situation.

kp.k: Mentoring is indispensable, with potential small-firm advantages
kp.d: Furlong argues that supervised practice, feedback, reflection and progressively greater participation in client conversations are essential to developing judgment. He asserts that mid-size and large firms generally perform this function poorly, while smaller firms have stronger incentives and opportunities for personal mentoring relationships. He also predicts that AI could decouple lawyer headcount from revenue, illustrating this with a future five-lawyer firm earning as much as a current hundred-lawyer firm.
qs: Law is something that I think really can only be learned with supervision and mentoring and guidance.
Smaller firms have to because you need to get that person providing value as soon as possible.
A five lawyer firm in the future could be generating the same kind of income that a hundred lawyer firm does today.
We need experienced lawyers to help new lawyers get over this, especially now to get over this period

kp.k: Verification can support quality control and judgment development
kp.d: Furlong recommends that small firms responsibly transfer production to AI while involving junior, other and contract lawyers in reviewing outputs, questioning problems and directing further checks. He distinguishes the immediate quality-control function from its developmental benefit for assessment and judgment. His suggestion that human checking may eventually become perfunctory is explicitly a prediction without a guarantee, not a demonstrated level of AI reliability.
qs: But not only is that quality control for the AI output, it is also the development of evaluative assessment judgment skills
transfer it from the people, humans doing it to machines doing it and humans evaluating it
at a certain point in all likelihood, no guarantee, but in all likelihood, the checking will become fairly perfunctory at some point down the road.

kp.k: Pair internal automation with scoped fixed or recurring fees
kp.d: Furlong recommends simultaneously changing internal production and external pricing. Firms should offer fixed service prices or recurring relationship arrangements, specify included work and identify events requiring a new discussion and fee. He frames the service around accompanying clients from uncertainty or difficulty toward clarity and resolution, rather than charging for the time and effort expended.
qs: I will do this for you every month. I will do this for you every quarter and you will pay me a set amount during that time.
Make a list of the stuff that you think is going to happen.
I’m not going to charge you for that separately. That’s part of our overall retainer agreement.
Change your internal workings, to increase your productivity by using technology, change your external pricing, and the relationships that go with it

kp.k: Forecast uncertainty makes professional values a strategic foundation
kp.d: Furlong explicitly qualifies the discussion as best guesses under uncertainty, rather than settled knowledge of the profession’s future. His closing recommendation is to gather the best available information and ground business adaptation in lawyers’ values, professionalism and integrity.
qs: And nobody knows for sure. Absolutely not. I mean, I don’t know for sure. We’re all making the best guesses we can.
That is your values as a lawyer. It’s your professionalism as a lawyer and it’s your integrity as a professional.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Furlong predicts a shift from lawyer-performed production to AI-operated workflows, with lawyers supervising, verifying outputs and advising clients.
pts.d: Jordan Furlong describes legal production as already moving away from extended human expert effort. In his forecast, AI becomes the conduit operating workflows, rather than merely receiving individual tasks. Lawyers monitor systems, validate outcomes and communicate their significance, adding judgment when clients request it. He recommends beginning this transfer now and predicts, with an explicit qualification, that verification may eventually become relatively perfunctory.

pts.k: Furlong expects AI production to weaken hourly pricing and shift firms toward outcome-, experience- and relationship-based fees.
pts.d: His reasoning is that work completed by AI in seconds cannot sustain the traditional pricing of human effort. He anticipates a much smaller role for hourly billing, while retaining it for selected novel or high-stakes advocacy. His recommended response is value pricing, fixed fees and recurring relationship arrangements, with explicit service scope and exceptions. This is both a prediction about pricing pressure and a prescription for adapting to it, not a reported finding about actual adoption rates.

pts.k: Furlong predicts that access to production systems will replace some staffing costs, lower and stabilise operating costs, and allow small lawyer headcounts to support much larger revenues.
pts.d: He envisages firms buying or renting workflow capabilities from software providers, naming Clio, Lexis and Thomson Reuters and speculating about OpenAI or Anthropic. These are possible system suppliers, not providers he identifies as already delivering this complete arrangement. He expects operating costs probably to decline and become more predictable. His five-lawyer-versus-hundred-lawyer comparison illustrates a possible future scale of revenue, not a measured productivity ratio. Although ownership and private equity frame the interview, he does not develop a concrete prediction about who will ultimately own the profit engine.

pts.k: Furlong predicts that AI will commoditise legal knowledge and capability, making personal reliability and client experience more important competitive differentiators.
pts.d: He forecasts AI surpassing even the most capable human lawyer within a few years, without defining a performance measure. Apart from very narrow specialisms, he argues that competing on expertise will consequently become less viable. Where lawyers have comparable AI capabilities and outcomes, he expects responsiveness and a better client experience to support premium pricing. He identifies integrity, trustworthiness and judgment under uncertainty as the enduring human offering.

pts.k: Furlong presents two possible client pathways: insured AI advice substitutes for lawyers, or AI analysis becomes an input to human counsel.
pts.d: He expects increasingly sophisticated AI to provide detailed advice to small-business users. The decisive condition is whether clients will trust that advice enough to act without a lawyer. He speculates that providers will eventually offer insurance or negligence recourse alongside AI advice; the monthly subscription and insurance prices in his example are hypothetical, not observed products. If clients accept that package as sufficient, he foresees potentially extensive displacement outside advocacy, especially preserving criminal advocacy. Alternatively, clients may bring AI analysis to a lawyer for a personal assessment. He expresses greater confidence in this second, human-in-the-loop pathway, while not ruling out substitution.

pts.k: Furlong argues that AI requires redesigning lawyer education and licensing around trustworthy judgment, supervised practice and client understanding.
pts.d: He says existing education and licensing will not serve the emerging role because AI can answer questions currently assigned to students and new lawyers. His proposal retains foundational legal knowledge, reasoning, analysis and issue spotting, but prioritises listening, interviewing, mentoring, reflection and progressively supervised client work. He also argues that verifying AI output can help develop lawyers’ assessment and judgment skills; the output-checking task and its educational benefit are distinct. He sees smaller firms as better positioned than larger firms to provide the necessary personal mentoring.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims are principally Furlong’s professional forecasts and conceptual arguments, supported by illustrative scenarios rather than empirical studies.
pts.d: Furlong identifies himself as a legal-sector analyst, consultant and forecaster. The transcript supplies no AI benchmarks, measured cost reductions, revenue comparisons, displacement data or documented insurance offerings supporting the predictions. Pricing and business-model arguments proceed from assumed rapid AI production, system-based costs and client preferences. His mentoring and interpersonal-skills arguments draw on professional observation and his experience as a journalist. The claims about education costs, duration and contribution to competence are asserted without a cited source. He explicitly acknowledges that the forecasts are uncertain.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Furlong anchors his account in February 2026, predicts expertise disruption within a few years, and leaves more radical substitution and verification changes undated and conditional.
pts.d: He describes the production shift as underway and recommends immediate responsible AI adoption and pricing changes. The prediction that AI becomes the smartest lawyer carries a 'few years' horizon. Reduced verification effort is only likely, not guaranteed, at an unspecified later point. Insurance-backed substitution is an eventual possibility conditional on product availability and clients’ willingness to rely directly on AI; he favours continued demand for human assessment. Pricing exceptions remain for some novel and high-stakes advocacy, and expertise-based competition may survive in very narrow areas. His recommendations answer a question about firms remaining successful in five or ten years, but he does not give all forecasts that deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The forecasts concern firm owners, employed and aspiring lawyers, clients and system suppliers, with particularly concrete implications for small firms.
pts.d: Owners face a shift from staffing-based production and hourly revenue toward system expenditure and scoped or recurring fees. Junior, other employed and contract lawyers move toward AI verification and client-facing judgment, while some production staffing may no longer be needed. Students and new lawyers require a different training pathway, and experienced lawyers become essential mentors. Small firms may combine substantially greater revenue capacity with an advantage in close supervision; Furlong says mid-size and large firms generally mentor less effectively. Clients, including small-business owners, may receive faster AI-generated analysis, choose between direct AI reliance and human counsel, and pay for outcomes and experience rather than time. Technology suppliers may become essential production-infrastructure providers. Advocacy, particularly criminal advocacy, is described as relatively protected in the severe displacement scenario.
